title: 12 follow up message templates that get responses
summary: Get 12 follow up message templates for meetings, proposals, and invoices, plus tips to write a follow up thank you email that gets replies.
body_markdown:
You send a great proposal, have a promising call, or meet someone useful at an event, and then... nothing. The deal stalls not because the client lost interest, but because no one sent the right follow up message at the right moment. A strong follow-up isn't about pestering people; it's a short, specific nudge that makes it easy for the other person to respond. Below are 12 templates for the most common situations freelancers and small teams face, from a follow up thank you email after a meeting to chasing an overdue invoice, plus the habits that make any follow-up land well. If you're also rethinking how you track who needs a nudge and when, it helps to first compare CRM (customer relationship management) tools built for follow-up tracking before picking a system to lean on.

## What makes a follow-up message actually get a response


Three things separate a follow-up message that gets a reply from one that gets ignored: timing, clarity, and personalization. Sending too soon feels pushy; waiting too long makes the message feel like an afterthought. A good rule of thumb is to match the urgency of the original conversation, a same-day note after a meeting, a few business days after a proposal.


Each follow-up also needs one clear ask. "Just checking in" rarely prompts action, but "Can you confirm the start date by Friday?" does. Finally, reference something specific from your last conversation, a detail, a name, a shared joke, so the message reads as personal, not copy-pasted.


## Follow up after a client meeting or call


The ideal time to send a follow up thank you email is within a few hours of the meeting, while the conversation is still fresh for both sides. This isn't just a courtesy note; it's a chance to put the agreed-upon details in writing so nothing gets lost or misremembered later. A good recap protects you if a client's memory of "what we decided" drifts a week down the line.


### Template 1: same-day thank you and recap


Subject: Great talking today, here's a quick recap


Hi \[Name\], thanks for the time today. Just to confirm what we landed on: \[decision 1\], \[decision 2\], and \[decision 3\]. Let me know if I missed anything, otherwise I'll move forward as outlined.


### Template 2: confirming action items


Subject: Next steps from our call


Hi \[Name\], to keep things moving, here's who owns what: I'll \[your task\] by \[date\], and you'll \[their task\] by \[date\]. Sound right?


## How to keep your follow-up messages on track


Remembering who needs a nudge works fine with three active clients. Past that, sticky notes and memory turn into missed follow-ups and, worse, duplicate ones that make you look disorganized. A shared record of your contacts, showing what was sent and when, is what actually keeps a pipeline moving, and it's worth learning how to keep track of clients effectively before your list outgrows a spreadsheet.


CRM tools like[Bonsai CRM](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/crm/) can automate reminders, but they're one option among several, not a requirement.


## Follow up after sending a proposal or quote


A proposal sitting unanswered for a week doesn't mean the client said no, it often just means they're busy or waiting on internal sign-off. The trick is nudging without sounding like you're chasing a decision. Wait a few business days after sending the proposal, then lead with a specific question rather than a generic check-in.


### Template 3: checking in after a proposal


Subject: Quick question on the proposal


Hi \[Name\], wanted to check if the scope and pricing in the proposal are clear, or if you'd like me to adjust anything before you decide. Happy to hop on a quick call if that's easier.


### Template 4: adding value before a decision


Subject: Something that might help


Hi \[Name\], while you're weighing this, I thought you'd find \[resource, example, or similar project\] useful. Let me know if it raises any new questions.

## Follow up when a client goes quiet


When a client stops responding, resist the urge to open with blame or a laundry list of unanswered emails. A stalled conversation usually means priorities shifted, not that the client is avoiding you, so the first re-opening message should feel low-pressure and easy to answer. If a contact has gone cold for weeks rather than days, it's worth learning how to write a re-engagement email that wins back clients before you send anything.


### Template 5: the light check-in


Subject: Still on your radar?


Hi \[Name\], no rush, just wanted to see if this is still something you're considering or if timing has shifted on your end.


### Template 6: the final follow-up


Subject: Closing the loop


Hi \[Name\], I'll go ahead and close this out for now, but feel free to reach back out whenever the timing works better. Wishing you well with \[project/goal\].


## Follow up on an unpaid invoice


An overdue invoice is rarely personal, most late payments come down to a busy inbox or a forgotten due date, not a refusal to pay. Start with the assumption of an oversight, then restate the amount and due date clearly so there's no confusion about what's owed. If the first reminder goes unanswered, it's fair to shift to a firmer, more direct tone on the second attempt. Tools like[Bonsai invoicing](https://www.zoom.com/en/products/bonsai/features/invoicing/) can help automate this sequence so reminders go out on schedule without you having to track due dates manually.


### Template 7: friendly payment reminder


Subject: Quick reminder: invoice #\[number\] due


Hi \[Name\], just a friendly note that invoice #\[number\] for \[amount\], due \[date\], hasn't come through yet. Let me know if you need another copy or if it slipped through the cracks.


### Template 8: firmer follow-up on a late invoice


Subject: Following up: invoice #\[number\] now \[X\] days overdue


Hi \[Name\], invoice #\[number\] for \[amount\] was due on \[date\] and is now \[X\] days past due. Please confirm a payment date this week, or let me know if there's an issue I should be aware of.


## Follow up after a networking conversation or introduction


A good networking follow-up does two things: it reminds the person exactly who you are, and it gives them a reason to keep talking. Mention something specific from your conversation, a shared connection, a detail about their work, so the message doesn't read like a mass send. Then suggest one concrete next step, a short call, a resource, an intro of your own, rather than leaving things open-ended.


### Template 9: thank you after a networking chat


Subject: Great meeting you at \[event\]


Hi \[Name\], really enjoyed hearing about \[specific topic\] earlier. Would love to continue the conversation, are you open to a quick call sometime next week?


### Template 10: following up on an introduction


Subject: Thanks for connecting us


Hi \[Name\], thanks to \[connector\] for the introduction. I'd love to learn more about \[their work or challenge\], happy to find 15 minutes whenever suits you.


## Follow up after a job application or sales pitch


Whether you're following up on a role or a pitch, the goal is the same: stay visible without sounding anxious. Reference the specific position or the exact value point you raised, not a generic "just checking in." Close with one easy next step, like your availability for a quick call, so the other person doesn't have to think about how to respond.


### Template 11: checking in after a job application


Subject: Following up on the \[role title\] application


Hi \[Name\], I applied for \[role title\] on \[date\] and wanted to reiterate my interest. Happy to answer any questions or hop on a call if that's helpful.


### Template 12: follow-up after a sales pitch


Subject: Following up on \[specific solution/topic discussed\]


Hi \[Name\], wanted to follow up on \[specific point from the pitch\] and see if it addresses what you're looking for. I'm free this week if a short call would help clarify anything.

## FAQ


### **Q1: How do you politely send a follow-up message?**


A polite follow-up message leads with the other person's time, not your own urgency. Open with a specific reference to your last conversation, keep the note short, and include a single clear ask so the reader knows exactly what to do next. Avoid phrases like "just checking in" without context, since they put the burden on the recipient to remember what you're referring to.


Tone matters as much as wording. A message that assumes good intent, such as noting a proposal or invoice "may have slipped through the cracks," reads as considerate rather than accusatory. That small shift in framing is often the difference between a follow-up that gets a reply and one that gets ignored.


### **Q2: What makes a good follow-up message?**


A good follow-up message combines three things: the right timing, a specific detail from the prior interaction, and one clear next step. Timing should roughly match the urgency of the original conversation, same day for a meeting recap, a few business days for a proposal check-in, and longer for a cold re-engagement note. Specificity signals that the message wasn't copy-pasted, and a single ask makes it easy to respond.


What a good follow-up avoids is just as important. Vague check-ins, multiple questions crammed into one note, and messages that ignore what was already discussed can reduce the odds of a reply. Templates help, but only when the placeholders are filled in with real details from the actual conversation.


### **Q3: How soon should you send a follow up thank you email after a meeting?**


The ideal window for a follow up thank you email is within a few hours of the meeting, while the details are still fresh for both sides. Sending it the same day also means any decisions or action items get documented before memory of the call starts to fade. Waiting more than a day or two makes the recap feel like an afterthought rather than a natural next step.


Beyond courtesy, a same-day thank-you email creates a written record of what was agreed. If a client's recollection of "what we decided" shifts a week later, that recap email is the reference point both sides can point back to.


### **Q4: How many follow-up messages should you send before stopping?**


Most situations call for two to three follow-up messages before stepping back: an initial nudge, one check-in a week or so later, and a final message that closes the loop without pressure. Beyond that point, additional messages tend to feel like pestering rather than genuine interest, especially if the recipient hasn't responded. A respectful final follow-up leaves the door open rather than demanding an answer.


The right number also depends on context. A proposal awaiting a decision might warrant a couple of gentle nudges, while an overdue invoice may need a firmer follow-up sooner since money owed is a different kind of urgency than a stalled sales conversation.


### **Q5: How does Bonsai help with follow-up messages?**


Bonsai CRM keeps clients and prospects organized on a pipeline with deal stages and notes, so it's easier to see who still needs a follow-up and who's already been contacted. Communication history lives on each contact record, and Zoom meeting transcripts can sync to that same record, giving a follow-up message real details to reference instead of a vague recap written from memory.


Bonsai proposals also add open and view tracking, so a freelancer can tell whether a client has actually looked at a proposal before deciding which follow-up template to send. None of this writes the message for you, but it removes the guesswork about timing and context that makes most follow-ups fall flat.


Twelve templates won't fix a follow-up habit that has no system behind it. Strong results come from pairing the right words with a clear view of who you've contacted, what you said, and when the next nudge is due. Bonsai's CRM and proposal tracking can hold that context for you, so many of your follow-up messages can be grounded in what actually happened, not just what you remember.
